::: {#exr-miller-deriv-opt-gamma-kernel}
#### Maximizing a gamma-family kernel

Adapted from @problifesavercalc, Question 1.1.10.

The [gamma distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_distribution)
is a standard model for positive, right-skewed quantities such as waiting times.
The gamma distributions form a family indexed by a shape parameter $a > 0$.
The [density](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pdf)
of the member with shape $a$ is [proportional](algebra.qmd#def-proportional)
to $x^{a-1} e^{-x}$ on $[0, \infty)$.
This factor is the density's kernel: the part that depends on $x$. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
The other factor is fixed and makes the density integrate to 1,
and finding it takes an integral. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->

Scaling a curve by a fixed factor does not move its peak,
so the kernel and the density have the same maximizer,
called the mode: the point where the density peaks.
Maximizing the kernel finds the mode without computing that factor.
That is useful whenever a density is known only up to such a factor,
as with many Bayesian posterior distributions.

For shape $a = 5$, the kernel is

$$f(x) = x^4 e^{-x}.$$

Find the [maximum](algebra.qmd#def-maximum) of $f$ on $[0, \infty)$.
:::

::: {#sol-miller-deriv-opt-gamma-kernel}
Differentiate using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)
&= 4x^3 e^{-x} - x^4 e^{-x} \\
&= x^3 e^{-x}(4 - x)
\end{aligned}
$$

On $[0, \infty)$, $e^{-x} > 0$, so $f'(x) = 0$ only at $x = 0$ and $x = 4$.

Evaluate $f$ at the boundary and critical points:

- At $x = 0$: $f(0) = 0$.
- At $x = 4$:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  f(4) &= 4^4 e^{-4} \\
  &= 256 e^{-4} \\
  &\approx 4.6888.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

- As $x \to \infty$: exponential decay dominates polynomial growth, so $\lim_{x \to \infty} x^4 e^{-x} = 0$.

Since $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \ge 0$ and $f(4) > 0$, the global maximum occurs at $x = 4$, with maximum value $256/e^4$.
:::
